title: I Choose You
hook: Lakshmi choosing Vishnu from the ocean of milk, and the line where the hymn stops saying 'her' and says 'you'
carry: prapatti: taking refuge is a choice
tomorrow: why is the fortune goddess's tree so hard to crack?

segments.voice: Yesterday painted her portrait: smiling, moist and blazing, satisfied and satisfying. Lakshmi's fortune is meant to flow outward.

A cover letter begins: to whom it may concern. Polite, careful, written to a title. Three paragraphs later, if the job matters enough, it starts to sound like a person talking to a person. A speech at a retirement party can go the same way: it starts about the colleague, and ends turned toward her, glass up, speaking to her directly. Something like that happens in the Sri Sukta today. For several lines the singer has talked about the goddess. Called her near. Described her. Then, at the end of one line, the pronoun changes.
screen: `TO WHOM IT MAY CONCERN.` → `A PERSON TALKING TO A PERSON.` → `THE PRONOUN CHANGES.`

segments.voice: A story first. The Bhagavata Purana tells that when Lakshmi rose from the churned ocean, she looked over the gods, sages and demons, found a flaw in each, and chose Vishnu, placing her garland on him. She chose. Today the Sri Sukta turns that around. Here's the line, in paraphrase. Bright as the moon, blazing with glory, Sri, cherished by the gods, generous: I take refuge in her, the lotus one. May misfortune be gone from me. I choose you. The first half is still the portrait. Then a step closer. I take refuge in her. Refuge is what you look for when you've run out of ways to manage on your own. The singer isn't only admiring her now; he's placing himself under her shelter. Then the request: may misfortune be gone. The word is Alakshmi, and she'll come back with a face of her own. And then the last two words. Tvam vrine. I choose you. All along it's been she, her, Sri. Suddenly it's you. The singer turns and speaks to her face to face. She chose once; now he chooses her. Here is the teaching. His words for refuge, sharanam prapadye, gave Hindus a name for a whole path: prapatti, surrender, taking refuge in God. In the Sri Vaishnava tradition of South India, devotees take refuge in Vishnu through Sri, honored as the mother who brings them in. Surrender, in this tradition, isn't giving up. It's choosing whom to turn to.
screen: `SHE CHOSE VISHNU.` · `I TAKE REFUGE IN HER.` · `MAY MISFORTUNE BE GONE.` · `PRAPATTI, TAKING REFUGE.` · then, large: `I CHOOSE YOU.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that's been weighing on you, a stretch of bad luck or a worry you keep circling, and let it be there. Then turn toward your shelter the way the hymn turns from her to you. If you pray, you can say the old words of refuge in your own language, 'I take refuge in you,' to the goddess, or to God, and rest there; if you don't, ask yourself gently where you go for shelter, a person, a place, a practice, and rest under it.
The Sri Sukta. The hymn where the singer takes refuge in Sri, asks for misfortune to go, and turns to say: I choose you.
Your line: prapatti, taking refuge is a choice. From she to you: the singer chooses where to turn. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: Some Hindus recite the Sri Sukta in full during Lakshmi worship at home or in temples, so this verse of refuge is spoken as part of the whole hymn.

Vishnu won't listen unless you pay Lakshmi first.
chat.meaning: The singer takes refuge in Sri and turns to her: I choose you. Sri Vaishnavas call that surrender prapatti, and they come to Vishnu through Sri.

notes: Verse 5 paraphrased: candrāṃ prabhāsāṃ yaśasā jvalantīṃ śriyaṃ loke devajuṣṭām udārām / tāṃ padminīm īṃ śaraṇam ahaṃ prapadye alakṣmīr me naśyatāṃ tvāṃ vṛṇe. Confirm 'cherished by the gods' for devajuṣṭām and 'generous' for udārām.

The claim that this is where the hymn first shifts to direct address ('the pronoun changes') should be checked against verses 1–4: verse 1 and 2 address Jatavedas (Agni) in the vocative, not Sri; verses 3–4 speak of Sri in the third person. Confirm 'for several lines the singer has talked about the goddess'.

vṛṇe glossed 'I choose'; the comparison to choosing a partner or a guide is an image, not a lexical claim (the verb is used of choosing a bride/groom and of choosing a priest in Vedic usage). Confirm.
Reading of the verse as the hymn's heart is attributed to 'some readers'; confirm.
